title: Event 1
content:
Summary Report: “Cloud Architect” Event Overview Event name: Cloud Architect Format: Team-based quiz game show Participants: 8 teams, each team with 5 members Topic: AWS cloud knowledge, architecture design, and some AWS Solutions Architect Associate (SAA)-style questions Registration: Google Form Team selection result: 19 June 2026 Event Objectives Create a new and engaging learning experience while keeping the spirit of sharing and studying Strengthen knowledge of Cloud, AWS, and solution architecture design Help participants review basic AWS architecture concepts through competitive questions Encourage teamwork, quick discussion, and confident decision-making under time pressure Practice risk management through special game skills Motivate interns to learn more about AWS Solutions Architect Associate (SAA) topics Event Format The event included 8 teams, and each team had 5 members Members did not need to be from the same internship group, but one person could not join more than one team Teams competed against each other in rounds Each match used question sets arranged from easy to difficult The team with the higher score advanced to the next round If both teams had the same score at the end, the tie-breaker used question 10 from an unused question set In this tie-breaker, the team that answered faster won the match Key Highlights AWS architecture quiz competition The game show used 10 question sets covering simple but practical AWS architecture topics Questions focused on cloud concepts, service selection, and solution design thinking Some questions were similar to AWS SAA exam scenarios, requiring participants to choose suitable AWS services or architecture patterns The format helped participants review theory in a more active way than normal reading or presentation sessions Teamwork and quick decision-making Each team had to discuss quickly before giving the final answer Members needed to divide thinking responsibilities, listen to each other, and agree under time pressure The competition format made teamwork more important because even simple questions could become difficult when the team was unsure Game skill: Minimum Risk Minimum Risk could be used once by each team This skill was useful for questions where the team was not fully confident If the answer was wrong, the team did not lose points If the answer was correct, the team received only half of the question’s score This skill encouraged teams to evaluate uncertainty before answering Game skill: Star of Hope Star of Hope could be used once by each team This skill was for the question the team felt most confident about If the answer was correct, the team received double points If the answer was wrong, the team lost double points This made the game more strategic because teams had to choose the right moment to take a risk Learning through competition The competitive format made the event exciting and easier to remember Participants could learn from both correct and incorrect answers The questions helped connect AWS theory with real architecture decision-making The event encouraged everyone to keep learning cloud fundamentals after the game Key Takeaways Cloud Knowledge AWS architecture design requires understanding not only individual services but also when to combine them SAA-style questions often focus on reliability, scalability, cost optimization, performance, and security Choosing the right service depends on requirements such as availability, latency, data storage, traffic, and operational effort Basic AWS knowledge becomes more useful when applied to scenario-based questions Team Strategy A good team needs both technical knowledge and clear communication It is important to discuss quickly but avoid rushing when the question includes important constraints Risk-based skills showed that not every question should be treated the same way Teams should use confident answers for high-reward opportunities and protect themselves when uncertainty is high Personal Development The event helped me recognize which AWS topics I already understood and which areas I need to review more Some SAA-related questions showed the importance of reading requirements carefully I learned that architecture decisions are often about trade-offs, not only memorizing services Practicing with a team helped improve confidence when explaining technical reasoning Applying to Work Review AWS core services such as compute, storage, database, networking, monitoring, and security Practice more SAA-style scenario questions to improve architecture design thinking When solving technical problems, identify requirements first before choosing a service Discuss options with teammates and explain the reason behind each architecture decision Apply risk management thinking when making choices under uncertainty Event Experience Participating in the “Cloud Architect” event was a fun and useful experience. The game show format made AWS architecture knowledge easier to review because every question required quick thinking, discussion, and decision-making.
Learning in an active way Instead of only listening to a presentation, participants had to actively answer questions The question sets helped review simple AWS concepts and architecture design principles SAA-style questions made the event more practical because they were close to real certification and project scenarios Working with a team Each team needed to combine the knowledge of all members Team discussion helped reduce mistakes and gave different perspectives for each question I learned that communication is very important when the team has limited time to decide Understanding risk and confidence The Minimum Risk skill taught me how to handle uncertain answers safely The Star of Hope skill showed the value and danger of overconfidence These mechanics made the event more exciting while also teaching a useful lesson about risk management Lessons learned Cloud architecture requires both knowledge and judgment Reading the question carefully is important, especially for AWS SAA-style scenarios Teamwork can improve answer quality when members share reasoning clearly Competitive learning can make technical knowledge more memorable and motivating Overall, the event helped me strengthen my AWS architecture foundation, practice teamwork, and understand how to make better technical decisions under pressure.

title: Event 2
content:
Summary Report: “FCAJ Community Day - June 2026” Event Overview Theme: “Data Driven, AI Risen” Community / organizers: AWS Study Group, First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ), Revve.ai, and CloudThinker Date & time: Saturday, 27 June 2026, 09:00 AM Venue: Bitexco Financial Tower, 2 Hai Trieu Street, Saigon Ward, Ho Chi Minh City Source: FCAJ Community Day - June 2026 Event Objectives Connect learners, cloud builders, AI engineers, and community mentors in the FCAJ ecosystem Share how a data-driven mindset supports practical AI adoption Introduce real-world perspectives from AI solution sales, founders, cloud engineers, and security builders Encourage participants to keep learning AWS, AI, cloud architecture, and security through community activities Inspire students and interns to build projects, join technical communities, and grow their professional network Speakers Truong Tran - AI Solution Sales, Noventiq Steve Tran - CTO / Founder, CloudThinker Trung Vu - CEO, Revve AI Anh Dang - Solution Sales, Noventiq Nghi Danh - AI Engineer, Renova Cloud Kiet Tran - AI Engineer, AWS Student Builder Group Bao Phan - Cloud Engineer, Cloud Kinetics Nguyen Nguyen - Cloud Engineer, Cloud Kinetics Toan Nguyen - AWS Security Builder Key Highlights Data-driven thinking as the foundation for AI The event theme emphasized that AI projects should start from data, business context, and measurable goals Good data preparation, clear problem definition, and practical use cases are important before applying AI tools A data-driven approach helps teams make better decisions instead of treating AI as only a trend Practical AI adoption in business and technology Speakers represented both business and technical roles, showing that AI adoption requires collaboration between sales, leadership, engineering, and security teams AI solution discussions highlighted the need to connect technology capabilities with business value The event encouraged participants to think about AI as a tool for solving real problems, improving workflows, and creating new products Cloud as the platform for modern AI AWS and cloud knowledge were positioned as important foundations for building scalable AI solutions Cloud engineers shared perspectives related to infrastructure, deployment, and operating modern workloads Participants were encouraged to continue learning cloud architecture, automation, and managed services Security and responsible building The presence of an AWS Security Builder highlighted the importance of security in AI and cloud projects AI systems should be designed with data privacy, access control, governance, and risk awareness in mind Security should be considered from the beginning instead of being added only after implementation Community learning and networking FCAJ Community Day created a space for learners to meet practitioners and understand different career paths The event connected students, engineers, founders, and AWS community members Community activities like this help participants gain motivation, ask questions, and discover learning roadmaps Key Takeaways Technical Mindset Start with data: AI quality depends heavily on the quality, availability, and meaning of data Use cloud foundations: AWS services and cloud architecture skills support scalable AI applications Build securely: Data-driven AI solutions must include security, privacy, and governance considerations Think end-to-end: A successful AI project covers data, model/use case, deployment, operations, and monitoring Career and Learning AI and cloud careers require continuous learning because tools and best practices change quickly Community events are valuable for understanding real industry expectations beyond classroom knowledge Learning from practitioners helps students and interns see how different roles work together in one project Networking with community members can open opportunities for mentorship, collaboration, and future projects Business Value AI should be connected to business goals, not implemented only because it is popular Data-driven decision-making helps teams evaluate impact more clearly Cross-functional collaboration between business and engineering teams is necessary to turn ideas into useful products Applying to Work Apply a data-first approach when analyzing requirements or proposing technical solutions When building AI-related features, clarify the target users, expected value, available data, and success metrics Continue improving AWS knowledge through labs, documentation, and community learning paths Include basic security checks early: data access, permissions, sensitive information, and deployment risks Practice explaining technical ideas in business language so that non-technical stakeholders can understand the value Event Experience Watching “FCAJ Community Day - June 2026” was useful because it showed how the AI and cloud community is growing around practical, real-world topics. The event did not focus only on technology buzzwords; it connected data, AI, cloud, business value, and career development.
Learning from diverse speakers The speaker lineup included founders, solution sales specialists, cloud engineers, AI engineers, and a security builder This diversity helped me understand that AI projects are not handled by only one role Each role contributes a different perspective: business needs, technical design, deployment, operation, and risk management Understanding the theme The message “Data Driven, AI Risen” reminded me that AI becomes meaningful when it is supported by the right data and clear objectives Before adopting AI tools, teams need to understand the problem, prepare data properly, and define what success looks like This mindset is useful for internship work because it encourages careful analysis before implementation Motivation for future learning The event encouraged me to keep learning AWS, cloud engineering, AI fundamentals, and security It also showed the value of joining communities like FCAJ to learn from real practitioners For future projects, I want to combine technical practice with better communication, documentation, and teamwork Overall, the event helped me see AI and cloud as practical tools that need strong data foundations, secure architecture, and collaboration between business and technical teams.

title: Event 3
content:
Summary Report: “AWS FCAJ Agent Forge - Deepdive” Event Overview Event name: AWS FCAJ Agent Forge - Deepdive Format: Online deep-dive learning session (theory + hands-on lab) Attendance date: Saturday, 01 August 2026, approximately 09:02–10:24 (UTC+7) Theory source: AWS FCAJ Agent Forge - Deepdive - YouTube Hands-on source: AgentForge - Ho Chi Min City Focus: Agentic AI architecture, AWS service integration, and practical implementation workflow Speakers Nghia Tran - Agentic SA Anh Pham - Cloud Consultant, G-AsiaPacific Vietnam Event Objectives Understand the core concepts behind an agentic AI system in AWS Learn how to structure an agent workflow from prompt design to tool usage Connect theory to practice through a step-by-step hands-on lab Strengthen practical skills in building, testing, and iterating AI agents Improve readiness to apply AI agents in internship tasks and future projects Key Highlights Theory: Agentic AI mindset and architecture The session emphasized that an AI agent is not only a chatbot, but a workflow that combines reasoning, tools, context, and action A strong architecture should separate concerns clearly: instruction layer, orchestration flow, data/tool integration, and output validation Prompt design should be structured, explicit, and outcome-oriented to reduce ambiguity during execution Retrieval, grounding, and context management are important to keep responses relevant and reliable Theory: Reliability, security, and operational thinking Building AI agents requires attention to reliability, not only model quality The event highlighted practical concerns such as access control, data safety, and permission boundaries Logging, observability, and evaluation loops are necessary for monitoring agent behavior and improving quality over time Responsible AI usage should include traceability and clear guardrails for unsafe or unsupported operations Hands-on Lab: Build and run an agent workflow The lab translated concepts into concrete implementation steps, from setup to execution Hands-on activities focused on creating and configuring an agent flow, connecting required resources, and running test scenarios The workflow showed how to iterate: run -> inspect outputs -> adjust prompts/configuration -> re-run The lab reinforced that practical quality comes from repeated validation, not one-time setup Key Takeaways Technical Learning Agent systems should be designed as end-to-end workflows, not isolated prompts Prompt quality directly affects consistency, actionability, and safety of outputs Tool integration must be explicit, controlled, and aligned with task scope Evaluation needs both functional checks (correctness) and operational checks (stability/safety) Engineering Mindset Start from requirements and expected behavior before choosing implementation details Keep iteration loops short and measurable when tuning prompts or logic Treat observability and error handling as first-class components of the solution Prefer repeatable patterns so the agent can be maintained and scaled by a team Applying to Work Apply structured prompt templates instead of ad-hoc prompts in internship tasks Use an iterative validation loop when building AI-related features: define criteria -> test -> refine Design agent tasks with clear boundaries on tools, data sources, and expected outputs Add basic logging and review checkpoints when automating technical workflows Document assumptions and constraints so teammates can reuse and improve the same workflow Event Experience Following “AWS FCAJ Agent Forge - Deepdive” was valuable because it connected architecture-level theory with implementation-level practice in one continuous flow.
What I found most useful The theory section gave a clear mental model for how an AI agent should be designed and operated The lab section turned that model into practical actions, making the concepts easier to internalize The combination of strategy (why) and execution (how) improved my confidence in building agent workflows Personal improvement points I need to keep improving prompt engineering discipline for more predictable outputs I should practice more evaluation scenarios to detect failure patterns early I should strengthen documentation habits so workflows are reproducible and team-friendly Overall, this event helped me move from a basic understanding of AI assistants to a more practical and engineering-oriented view of agent development on AWS.
